region: Central Thailand — Chao Phraya & Mae Klong floodplains
description: The short-finned wild ancestor of every pet-store betta, living in shallow, vegetated rice paddies, ditches and marshes. Males guard bubble nests and fight fiercely, which led Thai fanciers to breed them for fighting long before the long-finned show forms existed.

region: Southern Thailand & Peninsular Malaysia — swamps and paddies
description: Named the "peaceful" betta because males spar far less violently than B. splendens, so a pair can share a well-planted tank. Males are blue-green with a bright red crescent band near the margin of the tail.

region: Northeastern Thailand (Khorat Plateau) & Laos — Mekong basin
description: A bubble-nesting fighter of the Khorat Plateau whose males are covered in emerald-green iridescent scales, each one outlined in dark brown like a set jewel. It lives in shallow, densely vegetated paddies and swamps that shrink sharply in the dry season.

region: Samut Sakhon (Mahachai) & nearby coastal provinces west of Bangkok, Thailand
description: Described in 2012 from Nipa palm swamps near the coast, where males build bubble nests in the water-filled axils of palm fronds in slightly brackish water. The near-black body is covered in iridescent green scales, with two green bars on the gill cover and no red.

region: Eastern Thailand & Cambodia — shallow swamps and paddies
description: Described in 2012 for wild fighting fish east of the Chao Phraya. Males have a dark brown-to-black body, a black gill cover crossed by two red bars, and a red crescent edged in black at the tip of the tail.

region: Cambodia — Mekong basin lowlands
description: The smallest member of the splendens group, named from the Greek for "spotted" after the rows of round black marks on the male's dorsal fin. Males are brown-black flecked with green-blue iridescence, with black cross-bars on the tail.

region: Sumatra (Jambi) & Peninsular Malaysia (Johor) — peat swamp forest
description: A tiny wine-red betta of tea-coloured peat-swamp water whose pH can fall below 4.5. Males usually carry an iridescent green spot in the middle of the flank and build small bubble nests in sheltered nooks among the leaf litter.

region: Johor, Peninsular Malaysia — Ayer Hitam peat swamp
description: One of the smallest bettas and critically endangered, known from only a few peat-swamp sites in Johor that are being cleared for plantations. Males are almost entirely black, with only a faint blue-green iridescence on the fin margins.

region: Western Borneo (Kalimantan Barat) — blackwater peat swamps
description: A coccina-group betta from the blackwater swamps of West Kalimantan. Males are deep red peppered with iridescent green-blue scales over the rear of the body and fins, and spawn under a small bubble nest in a sheltered corner.

region: Central Kalimantan (around Palangkaraya), Borneo — peat swamps
description: Described in 2013, this coccina-group species stands out because the male's red body is almost entirely overlaid by metallic blue-green scales, so it can look turquoise in reflected light. It lives in acidic blackwater pools and swamp-forest streams.

region: Western Borneo (Kalimantan Barat) — blackwater peat swamps
description: A miniature coccina-group betta under 4 cm long whose males are an even, glowing red (rutilans means "reddish") with no iridescent spot on the flank. It hides among leaf litter in shallow, very soft and acidic swamp pools.

region: Sarawak, Borneo — peat swamp forest around Kuching
description: A small coccina-group betta from the peat swamps of western Sarawak; males are scarlet with a single iridescent green spot in the middle of the flank. Pairs spawn under a tiny bubble nest hidden in a sheltered spot near the surface.

region: Selangor, Peninsular Malaysia — North Selangor peat swamp forest
description: Endemic to the North Selangor peat swamp forest. Unlike B. coccina, both sexes carry the iridescent blue-green blotch on the flank, and the male's dark red body has a bluish, "livid" cast.

region: Bangka Island, Indonesia — blackwater peat swamps
description: Named after Burdigala, the Latin name for Bordeaux, for the claret colour of the males. A coccina-group betta known from acidic blackwater swamps on Bangka Island, where it shelters among leaf litter and roots.

region: Pahang & Terengganu, east coast of Peninsular Malaysia — peat swamps
description: A coccina-group betta from Malaysia's east coast. The male's red flanks are sprinkled with blue-green iridescent spots that continue onto the bases of the dorsal, anal and tail fins.

region: Peninsular Malaysia (Perak & Selangor) — peat swamp forest
description: One of the largest bubble-nesting bettas: a long, almost parallel-sided fish whose dark brown body is studded with an iridescent green mark on every scale. Males build big bubble nests among floating plants and can be quarrelsome, so it is usually kept in pairs.

region: Sumatra (Jambi & Riau) — blackwater peat swamps
description: A large, slender bubble-nester closely related to B. bellica, told apart by its slanted head profile and longer pelvic fins. Males build a large bubble nest among floating plants and show rows of metallic green scales over a dark brown body.

region: East Kalimantan, Borneo — shallow hill-forest streams
description: A dwarf paternal mouthbrooder: after spawning the male carries the eggs and fry in his throat for roughly two weeks. Males are rusty orange-red with black, white-edged dorsal, anal and tail fins — the "white seam" of its name.

region: East Kalimantan, Borneo — Mahakam basin forest streams
description: Named for its snakehead-like head, this dwarf paternal mouthbrooder lives among leaf litter in shallow forest streams of the Mahakam basin. Males are bright orange-red with black, white-edged dorsal and anal fins and a tail tipped in black and white.

region: Northern Borneo — Brunei & northern Sarawak hill-forest streams
description: A large, big-mouthed paternal mouthbrooder from cool, clear hill-forest streams of Brunei and northern Sarawak. Males are orange-red with a white-ringed black eyespot at the rear of the dorsal fin and bold black markings on the head.

region: Northeastern Borneo — Sabah & East Kalimantan forest streams
description: A large, torpedo-shaped mouthbrooder with a broad, snakehead-like head that lives in clear, flowing forest streams and is a notorious escape artist. Males have iridescent green-blue cheeks and fin streaks; the name refers to a single dark spot near the tail base.

region: Northern Borneo — Sabah & East Kalimantan forest streams
description: A large unimaculata-group mouthbrooder long confused with B. unimaculata, from clear forest streams of Sabah and East Kalimantan. Males show metallic green-blue scales on the cheeks and along the flanks, and like its relatives it is an accomplished jumper.

region: East Kalimantan, Borneo — forest streams around Balikpapan
description: A large paternal mouthbrooder from East Kalimantan whose colour varies by locality: fish from around Balikpapan show blackish bars on the body, while more northerly populations are reddish. Males are more strongly contrasted than females.

region: Peninsular Malaysia (incl. Penang) & southern Thailand — clear forest streams
description: A robust mouthbrooder of clear, flowing forest streams, where it lurks among submerged roots and marginal plants. Males have iridescent blue-green scales on the gill covers and a broad, lanceolate tail crossed by fine bars.

region: Bangka Island, Indonesia — forest streams
description: A pugnax-group mouthbrooder known only from Bangka Island. Males have a broader head than females, longer pelvic fins and the pointed central "spike" in the tail typical of the group.

region: Southeastern Thailand, Cambodia, Laos & southern Vietnam — forest swamps and streams
description: A small pugnax-group mouthbrooder ranging from Chanthaburi on the Gulf of Thailand into the Mekong basin and Phu Quoc Island. It forages along densely vegetated margins of clear streams and swamps; males are brown with green-blue iridescent spots on the gill cover and body.

region: Krabi Province, southern Thailand — limestone karst pools and streams
description: Unusual among bettas for living in hard, alkaline water: it is found only in clear, limestone-fed pools and streams around Krabi, and its tiny range makes it threatened. Males are brown with turquoise iridescent scales and blue-edged fins and carry the eggs in their mouths.

region: Java & Sumatra, Indonesia — hill streams, swamps and ditches
description: A small, hardy mouthbrooder that tolerates cooler upland water better than most bettas. Males are brown with two dark lengthwise stripes, and their anal and tail fins are bordered by a band of iridescent blue-green.

region: Western Borneo — Sarawak & West Kalimantan forest streams
description: A picta-group mouthbrooder of forest streams in western Borneo, brown with two dark lengthwise bands (taeniata means "banded"). Displaying males show iridescent blue-green scales on the gill cover and a bright turquoise edge to the anal fin.

region: Jambi Province, Sumatra — forest streams and swamps
description: A picta-group mouthbrooder from Jambi, named falx ("sickle") for the continuous curved outline the broad anal and tail fins make when a male displays. Males show a dark red-to-black line along the anal fin and a reddish band near the margins of the anal and tail fins.

region: Northern Sumatra (Aceh), Indonesia — forest streams
description: A rarely seen paternal mouthbrooder from northern Sumatra, described in 1893 but scarcely known alive until recent decades. Males are deep ruby-red to maroon with iridescent blue-green highlights in the fins, and incubate the eggs for about two weeks.

region: Sarawak & Brunei, northern Borneo — forest streams and swamps
description: Named for the Akar River in Sarawak, this large mouthbrooder lives in forest streams and swamps of northern Borneo. Mature males grow a lanceolate tail with greatly extended central rays, iridescent green-blue scales on the body and dark stripes before and behind the eye.

region: Southern Thailand & Peninsular Malaysia — peat swamp forest
description: A large waseri-group mouthbrooder named for the black mark on its throat, shaped like the Greek letter π. It lives in shaded blackwater peat-swamp creeks with deep leaf litter and tangled roots.

region: Peninsular Malaysia — blackwater peat swamps
description: The namesake of a group of large peat-swamp mouthbrooders recognised by their distinctive black throat markings and plain brown bodies. Males carry the eggs and fry in their mouths for around two weeks in tea-coloured, very acidic water.

region: Selangor & Perak, Peninsular Malaysia — blackwater peat swamps
description: Named after the horseshoe bats (Hipposideros) because the black mark on its throat is shaped like a horseshoe. Large adults favour flowing sections of blackwater streams, while smaller fish keep to quiet pools.

region: Central Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater swamp streams
description: A compact mouthbrooder from the blackwater of Central Kalimantan whose males carry two bright red bars on the gill cover. The rest of the body is a deep blue-black, with blue-green iridescence on the scales and fin margins.

region: Central Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater forest streams
description: A close relative of B. foerschi from Central Kalimantan, told apart by the golden rather than red bars on the gill cover. Like the rest of its group it is a paternal mouthbrooder of soft, acidic forest water.

region: West Kalimantan (around Mandor), Borneo — blackwater streams
description: A foerschi-group mouthbrooder from the Mandor area of West Kalimantan; like B. foerschi, the male has two red bars on the gill cover over a dark body. It lives in shaded, acidic blackwater streams and swamps.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Royal blue is the deepest of the three iridescent betta blues. Genetically it is the in-between form of steel blue and turquoise, so royal blue pairs never breed completely true.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Opaque white bettas carry a dense layer of white pigment cells over the body and fins, giving a porcelain look. Show-quality lines have no wash of red or blue anywhere.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Melano is a true, deep black caused by a recessive gene that greatly increases dark pigment. Melano females are notoriously poor breeders, so breeders usually pair melano males with black-lace or other females.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Yellow belongs to the "non-red" series, in which red pigment is suppressed and the body and fins turn butter-yellow. "Pineapple" fish show darker outlines around each scale.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A solid orange bred from the red and yellow (non-red) lines. Clean orange fish without red wash or stray iridescent scales are hard to fix and stand out at shows.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Turquoise (also sold as green) is one of the three iridescent betta colours, alongside royal and steel blue. The shade shifts from green to blue as the fish turns in the light.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Steel blue is the greyest, most metallic of the iridescent blues — a cool slate tone. Unlike royal blue it is homozygous, so steel-to-steel pairings breed true.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Plakat, from the Thai "pla kat" ("biting fish"), is the short-finned form kept for fish fighting long before show bettas existed. Short fins make it far more active and agile than long-finned varieties.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Made by crossing halfmoons into traditional plakats, giving a short tail with straight edges that still opens into a crisp 180° "D" when the male flares. It combines a plakat's vigour with the halfmoon show standard.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Developed in Indonesia in the late 1990s, crowntails have reduced webbing between the fin rays, so each ray projects like the point of a crown. Rays that branch two or more times give the fuller "double-ray" crowns breeders prize.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A recessive mutation splits the tail into two lobes and lengthens the dorsal fin base until it nearly matches the anal fin. Double tails also tend to have a shorter, deeper body.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: The original long-finned pet-shop betta: a flowing tail that droops down and back like a veil, spreading well under 180°. It remains the most common form in pet shops, though show breeders now favour fuller tails.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Delta-tailed bettas have a triangular tail whose edges flare straight outward to a spread clearly less than 180°. Deltas were an important step in the development of the super delta and halfmoon.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A super delta spreads its tail to between roughly 120° and just under 180° — fuller than a delta but short of a true halfmoon. Many halfmoon spawns produce super deltas among their offspring.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: An extreme halfmoon whose fin rays branch so many times that the tail edge ruffles like rose petals. The heavy finnage makes rosetails slow swimmers prone to fin damage.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A form between the veiltail and crowntail: the rays extend only moderately beyond the webbing, giving the fins a fringed, comb-like edge. Combtails often turn up in crowntail breeding lines.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: An uncommon tail type: a broad caudal that narrows evenly to a single point, like the spade on a playing card. It is closer in finnage to the wild type than most long-finned forms.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A halfmoon × crowntail cross: the tail still opens to about 180°, but the rays extend slightly past the webbing to give a finely serrated, sun-ray edge.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Derived from marble lines, koi bettas are patched in red, black and white like Nishikigoi carp. Because the marble trait is driven by a "jumping gene", the pattern often shifts as the fish ages.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A marble-derived line named after the cartoon clownfish, patched in vivid orange, red, yellow and black with little or no white. Like koi bettas, the pattern can keep changing through the fish's life.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A koi betta overlaid with scattered iridescent blue scales, so the red, black and white patches look dusted with stars. The speckling comes from adding iridescent (blue/turquoise) genes to koi lines.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Generally traced to crosses with wild Betta mahachaiensis, dragon scales grow a thick metallic-white coating over each scale like armour plating. When overdone the coating can spread over the eyes and blind the fish.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A Thai-developed line selected purely for size, reaching around twice the length of an ordinary betta. Giants grow quickly and need more space and food than standard plakats.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A bicolour with a dark blue-to-green body and yellow-to-orange fins, usually separated from the body colour by a dark blue band at the fin base. It was created by combining blue (iridescent) and yellow (non-red) lines.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A near-black betta whose fins carry steel-blue iridescent streaks along each ray, giving a dark, orchid-petal effect. It combines black (melano or black-lace) genes with steel-blue iridescence and is usually bred as a halfmoon.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Copper bettas carry heavy metallic iridescence, generally traced to crosses with wild B. mahachaiensis, that covers body and fins with a glinting copper-gold sheen. Under some lighting the same fish flashes blue or purple.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A metallic white produced by combining metallic and iridescent genes until the body and fins look like polished silver. It is brighter and more reflective than an opaque white.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Cellophane bettas lack nearly all pigment, so their fins are clear and pale pink flesh shows through the body. They are not albinos — their eyes stay dark.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: In the butterfly pattern each fin has a solid inner colour that ends in a sharp, pale outer band; ideally the boundary falls at half the fin's length. Blue-and-white is the classic combination.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Marble bettas carry a transposon ("jumping gene") that keeps switching pigment on and off, so their blotchy pattern can change completely over a lifetime. Many start pale and darken, or the reverse.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: Named for its hugely enlarged pectoral fins, often white, which flap like elephant ears as the fish hovers. The trait is recessive, and the big fins make dumbos weaker swimmers than ordinary halfmoons.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: One of the oldest colour forms: a pale, flesh-coloured body with solid red fins, produced by the loss of dark pigment and iridescence from the body while red stays in the fins.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: central Thailand floodplains)
description: A dragon-scale line on a black base: thick metallic blue-silver scales, each outlined in black, give the body an armoured, samurai-like look while the fins stay dark.

region: India, Bangladesh & Pakistan — slow, heavily vegetated rivers, lakes and ditches
description: Males build sturdy bubble nests reinforced with bits of plant and guard the eggs and fry alone. Wild-type males are crossed by slanting bands of red-orange and iridescent blue, with a turquoise throat.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: India & Bangladesh)
description: A line-bred dwarf gourami in which the iridescent blue bands have spread over almost the whole male, leaving only faint traces of red. Females remain silvery grey.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: India & Bangladesh)
description: Bred for maximum red: the male is solid flame-red to orange from snout to tail, keeping blue only on the throat and dorsal fin. Females stay silvery.

region: Northeastern India & Bangladesh — vegetated ponds, lakes and ditches
description: One of the most peaceful gouramis. In breeding dress the male turns honey-orange with a sooty black face, throat and belly and a lemon-yellow dorsal fin; females and resting males are silvery-brown with a dark lengthwise stripe.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: northeastern India & Bangladesh)
description: The honey gourami usually sold today: a xanthistic line in which both sexes are golden yellow and males lack most of the black throat colour, deepening to rich orange when breeding.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: northeastern India & Bangladesh)
description: A deeper red-orange line bred from gold honey gouramis; males glow red-orange from snout to tail while females are a paler orange.

region: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh & Myanmar — rivers, ponds and ditches
description: A larger cousin of the dwarf gourami: greenish-silver, crossed by slanting orange and blue-green bands. Breeding males darken, with a red-edged anal fin and blue-black throat, and build a large bubble nest.

region: Southern Myanmar — Irrawaddy & Sittang basins
description: Named for the male's thickened lips, this Burmese gourami looks like a stockier banded gourami. Males are brown-orange with faint blue bars and a red-edged anal fin, and build bubble nests among floating plants.

region: Mekong basin & Sundaland — Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, Malaysia & Indonesia
description: Hardy and adaptable, it is named for two dark spots on the flank, with the eye counted as the third. Its long, thread-like pelvic fins carry taste cells and are used to feel through vegetation.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mekong basin & Sundaland)
description: The common blue strain of the three-spot gourami, selected for an even steel-blue body with darker, marbled crossbars; the two black body spots remain.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mekong basin & Sundaland)
description: A xanthistic strain of the three-spot gourami: black pigment is lost, so the body turns golden with faint darker marbling and the two body spots disappear.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mekong basin & Sundaland)
description: The opaline or "Cosby" strain is light blue overlaid with heavy, dark blue marbling across the flanks in place of the wild-type spots and bars.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mekong basin & Sundaland)
description: A pale, silvery-white strain of the three-spot gourami with a pearly sheen and little or no pattern. Its iris keeps the species' orange-red colour.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins — Thailand, Cambodia & Vietnam: swamps and lakes
description: A plain but elegant gourami whose tiny scales give its silvery body a soft, moonlit sheen. Breeding males develop orange-red pelvic threads and build large nests of bubbles and plant fragments.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins; introduced widely — swamps and rice paddies
description: The largest Trichopodus, farmed across Southeast Asia as a food fish and sold dried in Thailand as "pla salid". Named for the zig-zag oblique bars and broken dark stripe that recall snakeskin.

region: Sundaland — Sumatra, Java, Borneo & the Malay Peninsula; farmed widely
description: A huge, long-lived gourami farmed for food across Southeast Asia; old males develop a bulging forehead hump and thick lips. Pairs build a spherical nest of plant material rather than a simple bubble nest.

region: Sabah, northern Borneo — Kinabatangan & neighbouring rivers
description: A Bornean giant gourami that keeps striking colours into adulthood: a dark grey-brown body with a broad red margin to the tail and other unpaired fins. Adult males develop a pronounced forehead hump.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — peat-swamp blackwater
description: A delicate peat-swamp gourami that needs very soft, acidic, warm water. Unusually for a gourami the female, not the male, broods the eggs in her mouth for about two weeks.

region: Western Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater swamps
description: Shows reversed sexual dimorphism: the female is the showy one, turning brick-red with green-blue bands when courting, while the male stays brownish. The male broods the eggs in his mouth, his throat distending to hold them.

region: Southern & Central Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater swamps
description: A chocolate gourami from the blackwater swamps of southern Borneo (selatan means "south"), chocolate-brown crossed by thin pale bands. Like its relatives it is a mouthbrooder that needs very soft, acidic water.

region: Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater swamps
description: The largest Sphaerichthys, with a pointed, upturned mouth. The male broods the eggs; displaying females show a dark spot behind the head and vertical stripes over a yellowish belly, while males may show a horizontal stripe.

region: Myanmar — vegetated streams and lake margins of the Irrawaddy basin
description: A tiny, rarely kept relative of the chocolate gouramis, grey-brown with a large gold-ringed dark eyespot in the middle of the flank. It is delicate in captivity and has rarely, if ever, been bred.

region: Bangka Island, Indonesia — blackwater peat swamps
description: The first licorice gourami to be described, from blackwater swamps on Bangka. Males have a lanceolate tail with a filament-like central ray; many fish sold under this name are actually other species, such as the round-tailed P. bintan.

region: Central Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater swamps
description: Like all licorice gouramis it spawns upside-down in a tiny cave, sticking the eggs to the roof beneath a few bubbles. Males take longer than most species to develop their full fin colours of red-brown, black and iridescent blue.

region: Peninsular Malaysia — peat swamp forest
description: A Malaysian licorice gourami whose males display broad red and black bands edged in iridescent blue on the dorsal, anal and tail fins. Males and females look much alike until they are well grown.

region: West Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater swamps
description: Named for the ornately banded tail: the male's rounded caudal fin carries bands of red-orange, black and iridescent blue. It lives among leaf litter in shallow, extremely soft blackwater.

region: Southern & Central Kalimantan, Borneo — blackwater swamps
description: Distinguished by a lanceolate tail with a long, unbranched central filament and by reddish unpaired fins banded in black and blue. Like other licorice gouramis it spawns in tiny caves and needs very acidic water.

region: Eastern Peninsular Malaysia — peat-swamp streams
description: Displaying males turn very dark, with a black band through the dorsal, anal and tail fins bordered on both sides by iridescent blue, and emerald-green pelvic fins. It lives in acidic peat-swamp streams of eastern Peninsular Malaysia.

region: Mainland Southeast Asia & Sundaland — paddies, ditches and swamps
description: Makes audible croaking sounds by snapping specialised tendons over its pectoral fin rays during displays. It is brownish-olive with dark lengthwise stripes, iridescent blue eyes and red- and blue-flecked fins.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Malay Peninsula & Sumatra — vegetated swamps and ditches
description: One of the smallest gouramis, its fins and flanks spangled with iridescent blue-green and red dots. Males croak audibly when displaying, and the bubble nest is built beneath a leaf rather than at the open surface.

region: Thailand, Laos & Cambodia — middle Mekong basin
description: A croaking gourami with three bold dark lengthwise stripes, from the middle Mekong basin. Like its relatives, males make audible croaking sounds with their pectoral fins during displays.

region: Northeastern India & Bangladesh — Ganges & Brahmaputra floodplains
description: A slender, angular-headed gourami with a pointed snout and large mouth, brown with an interrupted silvery-white stripe from the eye to the tail. The male broods the few, large eggs in his mouth and turns a marbled pattern while brooding.

region: Sri Lanka — wet-zone forest streams
description: Endemic to Sri Lanka, this robust, territorial labyrinth fish is named for the comb-like fringe of extended rays on its tail. The male builds a bubble nest under a leaf or rocky overhang and guards the eggs, driving off even the female.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java & Borneo — rivers and swamps
description: The larger of the two combtails: greyish-brown with a dark net pattern over the scales and comb-like ray extensions on the tail. A hardy but rather predatory bubble-nester that needs a large tank.

region: Sri Lanka — shaded wet-zone forest streams
description: A small, secretive Sri Lankan endemic whose males carry long, pointed extensions on the dorsal, anal and tail fins. It lives among leaf litter and roots in shaded rainforest streams and spawns under a small bubble nest in a sheltered spot.

region: Southern & eastern China, Taiwan, Korea & northern Vietnam — paddies, ponds and slow streams
description: One of the first ornamental fish kept in Europe (imported to France in 1869), it thrives in unheated water. Males are banded blue and red-orange, with a dark, orange-ringed spot on the gill cover and long, forked tail streamers.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern China & Taiwan)
description: A long-established albino strain: dark pigment is missing, leaving a cream body crossed by pale red-orange bands and pink eyes. It is just as hardy and quarrelsome as the wild form.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern China & Taiwan)
description: A strain in which red pigment is suppressed, leaving the body and fins in shades of blue to blue-black with darker bars. The opercular spot and long tail streamers of the wild form remain.

region: Eastern China & Korea — ponds, paddies and ditches
description: Probably the most cold-tolerant labyrinth fish, surviving winters at around 5 °C in its native ponds and paddies. Unlike the common paradise fish it has a rounded tail and is brownish without bold bars.

region: Northern Vietnam — ponds and slow streams
description: Long sold as M. concolor, the black paradise fish is dark grey-brown to almost black, with a forked tail whose filamentous rays carry white or black tips over blue membranes. It lacks red in the unpaired fins, unlike the similar M. erythropterus.

region: Southern India & Sri Lanka — coastal swamps, paddies and ditches
description: A small, hardy labyrinth fish whose rounded tail ends in a short central point. Breeding males turn deep red-brown with blue-edged fins and spawn under a small bubble nest, often in a cave or beneath a leaf.

region: Southwestern India (Kerala) — coastal swamps and ditches
description: Brown with two dark lengthwise stripes, it has extended central tail rays and blue-edged fins with a red band inside the margin. Pairs spawn under a small bubble nest in a sheltered spot and the male guards the eggs.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Bangka, Belitung & Borneo — blackwater swamps and streams
description: A slender ambush predator that hangs motionless among vegetation, then shoots out an enormously protrusible mouth to engulf small fish. Although it belongs to the gourami family it has only a simple air-breathing chamber rather than a true labyrinth, and it is a mouthbrooder.

region: Thailand, Cambodia, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java & Borneo — sluggish rivers and swamps
description: Famous for "kissing" bouts in which two fish press their lips together — actually a trial of strength between rivals. The lips bear horny teeth for rasping algae, and fine gill rakers strain plankton; it scatters floating eggs without building a nest.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Southeast Asia)
description: The familiar pink kisser is a leucistic farmed strain with a pinkish-white body and clear fins; its eyes stay dark. It behaves exactly like the green wild form, grazing algae and sparring lip-to-lip.

region: South & Southeast Asia — India to southern China, Indonesia & the Philippines: swamps, paddies and canals
description: A tough air-breathing perch that can survive out of water for days and moves overland between pools, levering itself along with its spiny gill covers and fins. It is an important food fish across South and Southeast Asia.

region: Congo River basin, Central Africa
description: A patient ambush predator from the Congo basin that drifts slowly, head angled down like a dead leaf, before snapping up small fish. Its tan body is covered in dark leopard spots, with a dark spot at the tail base.

region: West & Central Africa — Senegal to the Congo basin
description: A robust grey-brown bushfish with a dark, pale-ringed spot at the tail base, found in rivers and swamps across West and Central Africa. Pairs spawn at night without a nest, releasing thousands of oily, floating eggs that receive no care.

region: Congo River basin, Central Africa
description: Named for the ringed eyespot near its tail, this Congo bushfish is mottled brown with darker bands. Like its relatives it is a stealthy predator that lurks among roots and plants in dim water.

region: Lower Congo basin & Chiloango River, Central Africa — forest streams
description: Settled adults glow orange-red crossed by dark bars, and mature males grow white-edged, extended dorsal and anal fins. The male builds a small bubble nest among plants at the surface, much like a paradise fish.

region: Congo River basin, Central Africa — swampy forest streams
description: A small bubble-nesting bushfish whose tan-to-brown body is crossed by dark vertical bars. Males grow longer, pointed dorsal and anal fins and guard the nest and eggs alone.

region: Central Africa — Cameroon to the Congo basin: dim forest streams
description: A small, shy bushfish of shaded forest streams, dark brown with indistinct darker bars. Males build a bubble nest at the surface and guard the eggs.

region: Southern China & Taiwan — hill streams, ponds and ditches
description: A hardy, cool-tolerant snakehead with no pelvic fins, olive-brown with dark chevrons, fine pale spots and a ringed eyespot at the tail base. Pairs guard a mass of floating eggs and then the fry at the surface.

region: Upper Brahmaputra basin, Assam (India) & Bhutan
description: A dwarf snakehead with no pelvic fins, a brilliant orange-red wash on the lower flanks, a blue-speckled body and orange-edged fins. Unlike its look-alike C. andrao it guards floating eggs rather than mouthbrooding, and it does best in cool water.

region: Northern West Bengal & Assam, India — swamps of the Brahmaputra basin
description: Described in 2013 from the Lefraguri swamp in West Bengal, it is one of the smallest snakeheads at around 10 cm. It lacks pelvic fins and, unlike the similar C. bleheri, is a mouthbrooder; the unpaired fins carry an electric-blue margin.

region: Rakhine State, western Myanmar — hill streams
description: Described in 2007, a grey dwarf snakehead peppered with black dots and patched with reddish-orange, with semicircular white bands on the pectoral fins. The male picks up the floating eggs and broods them in his mouth while the female guards the territory.

region: Rakhine State, western Myanmar — Waloun Chaung hill streams
description: Told apart by the large black spots on its cheeks, golden-orange lips, red rim to the gill cover and 5–7 alternating white and dark bands on each pectoral fin. Its body scales are a mix of red and bluish-grey, peppered with black spots.

region: Assam & northeastern India — hill streams and tea-garden channels
description: A dwarf snakehead of Assam's hill streams, chocolate-brown with broken dark bars and orange-edged unpaired fins. The male broods the eggs and young in his mouth for two to three weeks.

region: South Asia — India, Bangladesh & neighbouring countries: hill streams, ponds and ditches
description: A small, hardy snakehead with orange-edged dorsal, anal and tail fins over a dark olive-grey body. The male broods the eggs and fry in his mouth, and the female feeds the young with infertile "trophic" eggs.

region: South Asia — Pakistan to Bangladesh & Sri Lanka: swamps, ponds and paddies
description: A tough, widespread South Asian snakehead that can survive the dry season buried in damp mud. Olive-brown with dark spots and blotches, it guards its floating eggs and fry at the surface.

region: South & Southeast Asia; widely farmed and introduced — swamps, paddies and rivers
description: One of the most important food fishes of South and Southeast Asia, able to survive in the mud of drying swamps by breathing air. Both parents guard the orange-and-black fry as they shoal at the surface; adults are brown with dark chevron bars.

region: Mekong basin & Sundaland — forest streams and peat swamps
description: A slender, long-snouted snakehead of shaded forest streams and peat swamps, tan with a row of dark blotches along the side and darker mottling above. Its pike-like head suits a patient hunter among dense, overhanging cover.

region: Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater rivers and swamps
description: A Sundaland snakehead with two or three large, orange-ringed black eyespots along each flank and another at the tail base. It lives in slow blackwater rivers and swamps and is seldom bred in captivity.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo & Palawan — blackwater swamps and forest streams
description: A dark, almost uniformly black-brown snakehead of acidic blackwater swamps and forest streams in Sundaland; melasoma means "black body". It hides among roots and leaf litter by day.

region: Upper Brahmaputra basin, Assam, India (type locality Dibrugarh)
description: Endemic to the upper Brahmaputra, its dark brown-to-black upper body bears seven or eight large, irregular orange blotches. The pectoral fins are boldly banded in black.

region: Upper Brahmaputra floodplains — Assam (India) & Bangladesh
description: A prized and very expensive snakehead that lives in burrows in the mud banks of the Brahmaputra floodplain. It is dark above with black spots crowding the upper flanks, a pale unspotted belly and red-edged dorsal, anal and tail fins.

region: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka & Bangladesh — deep rivers, lakes and reservoirs
description: A giant predatory snakehead named for the large, orange-ringed black "bullseye" at the base of the tail. It exceeds a metre in the wild, and both parents fiercely guard the floating eggs and fry.

region: Mainland Southeast Asia & Sundaland — large rivers, lakes and reservoirs
description: The largest snakehead, sold as the "red snakehead" when young for its orange juveniles banded with two black stripes. Adults turn blue-black above and pale below and defend their floating eggs and fry ferociously.

region: China, Korea & the Russian Far East (Amur & Yangtze basins); invasive in the USA
description: A cold-hardy snakehead that tolerates near-freezing water and breathes air in stagnant ponds. Tan with large, dark, python-like blotches; its spread through U.S. waters made it a notorious invasive species, and keeping it is banned in many places.

region: West & Central Africa — Senegal to the Congo basin, Lake Chad & upper Nile
description: An African snakehead of swamps and slow, vegetated rivers, olive-brown with a row of dark blotches along the side and dark lines behind the eye. Like Asian snakeheads it breathes air, and pairs guard their floating eggs.
